passage: In the small-town college at Tonk, the girls' bus had been cancelled for a month and nobody in charge seemed to care. Nazia, twenty, stood for student union president. At first it was about the bus. She loved the feeling when juniors called her "Nazia-di" and asked what she thought. After winning, she got the bus back in two weeks and everyone cheered. Then she noticed she was deciding everything: the fest theme, the posters, even who stood at the gate. At a meeting Bidisha, her closest friend, said quietly, "You didn't ask anyone about the theme." Nazia felt her face flush. She wanted to snap back. Instead she said, "You're right. Let's vote." It stung. She knew it was the right sting.

qa.q: How long did it take Nazia to get the bus back?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Bidisha pointed out she hadn't asked anyone?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and defensive, with her face flushing and an urge to snap back.

qa.q: What turning point kept Nazia's influence serving the group?
qa.a: Nazia chose to admit Bidisha was right and call a vote, instead of snapping back, which stopped her slide into controlling everything.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see Nazia's time as president?
qa.a: Bidisha likely admires how Nazia fixed the bus, but worries about her deciding everything alone, which is why Bidisha spoke up.

grounding: A young woman seeks student leadership to fix a real problem and enjoys the respect, then notices herself sliding toward control.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: Lindiwe had wanted to be head of the residence council at her university in Durban since first year. When she won, the respect felt like sunlight: people stopped her on the stairs to ask her opinion, and the warden began to call her by name. She fixed the broken laundry machines within a week. Then she began choosing every committee member herself, people who agreed with her. Sami, the quiet engineering student on her floor, came to her door. "You picked all your friends. Some of us feel we don't have a voice anymore." Lindiwe's first thought was to defend herself. Her second was worse: she liked that nobody argued. That thought scared her. She opened the committee list again and added two open seats.

qa.q: What did Lindiwe fix within a week?
qa.a: The broken laundry machines.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe's second thought scare her?
qa.a: She realised she enjoyed that nobody argued with her, and she worried that her wish for influence was turning into a wish for control.

qa.q: What choice did Lindiwe make after Sami's visit, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She added two open seats to the committee, giving others a voice again instead of keeping all the power with her friends.

qa.q: How were students like Sami affected by Lindiwe's early choices?
qa.a: They felt shut out, as if they no longer had a voice in the residence, which is why Sami came to her door.

grounding: A young woman gains student leadership, enjoys influence and respect, and catches herself sliding toward control.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: The hostel mess committee election was a bigger deal than it sounded, and Nitin campaigned hard. He wanted the food fixed, but he also wanted the respect: juniors saluting him in the corridor, the warden asking his opinion. He won by forty votes. In his first month he got fresh chapatis at dinner and fixed the water cooler. Everyone loved him. In his second month he banned late plates without asking anyone and told the cooks to report only to him. Hafsa, the committee treasurer, stopped him outside the office. "People who work late can't eat now. You didn't ask us." Nitin felt a sharp flash of irritation. Then he saw two tired lab students walking past with empty hands. He cancelled the ban that evening.

qa.q: By how many votes did Nitin win?
qa.a: By forty votes.

qa.q: What does Nitin's flash of irritation at Hafsa suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he had started enjoying control and felt challenged when someone questioned his decision.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Nitin choose?
qa.a: Seeing two tired lab students walking past with empty hands, Nitin saw the real cost of his ban and chose to cancel it that evening.

qa.q: How might the students who work late have felt about the ban?
qa.a: They would have felt ignored and frustrated, going hungry because of a rule nobody asked them about.

grounding: A young man seeks hostel leadership for good changes and respect, slides into control, then corrects course.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage:
Subject: I won, and something's bothering me

Afreen Apa,
You'll have seen my photos. Your little brother is head of the cultural committee now. I stood because the fest was always run by the same three seniors and nobody else got a say. I wanted juniors and day scholars to have a voice.
And honestly, I love it. The principal calls me by name. People ask what I think before they decide things. It feels like standing a little taller.
But here's what's bothering me. Yesterday a first-year, Tanya, booked the auditorium for a poetry night without asking me first. My first thought was, cancel it. Who does she think she is? I actually had the email typed.
Then I remembered: that's exactly what I stood against.
I didn't send it. I went to her event instead, and it was good.
Apa, how do you want respect without wanting to control everyone? Tell me when you call on Sunday.
Zubin

qa.q: What did the first-year, Tanya, book without asking?
qa.a: The auditorium for a poetry night.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he typed the email to cancel the poetry night?
qa.a: He felt his authority was challenged and wanted to assert control, as if Tanya had disrespected his new standing.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Zubin, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Remembering that he stood against a few people controlling everything made him not send the email, keeping his influence in service of the group.

qa.q: How might Tanya have experienced it if Zubin had cancelled her event?
qa.a: She would likely have felt shut out and discouraged, as if a new leader had become just another gatekeeper.

grounding: It shows a young adult who seeks student leadership to shape decisions and be respected, and notices his wish for influence sliding toward control.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage:
"You want the honest version, Aparna? Okay, for the college paper.
I stood for the university senate because we women in our hostel had a curfew at eight and men had none. Nobody on the senate had ever lived with that rule. I thought, if I'm in the room, it changes.
And it did. We got it moved to ten, same for everyone. Girls I didn't know stopped me in the canteen to thank me. I won't lie, that felt wonderful.
But you should also print this. After a few months I noticed I liked being in the room more than what happened in it. I liked the dean saying, 'Rukmini, what do you think?' I started speaking in meetings even when I had nothing to add, just so they'd remember me.
So now I keep a card in my bag. It says: who is this for? Before every meeting, I read it."

qa.q: What does the card in Rukmini's bag say?
qa.a: Who is this for?

qa.q: What worried Rukmini about herself after a few months on the senate?
qa.a: She was worried that she had come to enjoy being in the room and being asked her opinion more than the decisions themselves.

qa.q: What choice has Rukmini made to keep her influence serving others?
qa.a: She carries a card asking 'who is this for?' and reads it before every meeting, to check that she speaks for the students rather than for her own standing.

qa.q: How might the girls in the hostel see Rukmini's time on the senate?
qa.a: They likely see her as someone who used her position to win them fairer rules, and are grateful.

grounding: It shows a young adult who seeks a senate seat to shape decisions and gain respect, uses it for the group, and guards against wanting standing for its own sake.
